paragraphs: I

Even now, the canons gossip a great deal among themselves about a hidden treasure belonging to this Abbot Thomas. The people of Steinfeld have often searched for it, though so far without success. They say that Thomas, while still in the prime of life, buried an enormous quantity of gold somewhere around the monastery. When repeatedly asked where it was, he would answer with a laugh, ‘Job, John, and Zechariah will tell either you or those who come after you.’ Sometimes he added that he would not begrudge it to whoever found it. Among this abbot’s other works, I think one especially deserves to be remembered. He filled the great window at the eastern end of his church’s south aisle with beautifully painted figures in glass, as his own portrait and coat of arms there demonstrate. He also restored almost the whole of the abbot’s house, digging a well in its courtyard and decorating it with beautifully carved marble. He died somewhat suddenly in his seventy-second year, in the year of Our Lord 1529.

“I suppose I’ll have to translate this,” the antiquary said to himself as he finished copying these lines from the rather rare and excessively long-winded Sertum Steinfeldense Norbertinum. “Well, I may as well do it now as later.” He quickly produced the following translation:

To this day, the canons gossip a great deal about a hidden treasure belonging to this Abbot Thomas. The people of Steinfeld have often searched for it, but so far without success. The story is that Thomas, while still in the prime of life, hid a very large quantity of gold somewhere in the monastery. When asked where it was, as he often was, he always answered with a laugh, ‘Job, John, and Zechariah will tell either you or your successors.’ Sometimes he added that he would bear no grudge against whoever found it. Among this abbot’s other works, I should particularly mention the great window at the eastern end of the church’s south aisle. He filled it with beautifully painted figures in glass, as his portrait and coat of arms in the window confirm. He also restored almost the whole of the abbot’s house and dug a well in its courtyard, which he decorated with beautiful marble carvings. He died rather suddenly in his seventy-second year, A.D. 1529.

The antiquary’s task at that moment was to trace the whereabouts of the painted windows from Steinfeld’s abbey church. Shortly after the Revolution, a great quantity of painted glass came to this country from the dissolved abbeys of Germany and Belgium. It can now be seen decorating various parish churches, cathedrals and private chapels here. Steinfeld Abbey was one of the largest involuntary contributors to our artistic possessions. I am quoting the rather ponderous introduction to the antiquary’s own book. Most of the glass from that abbey can be identified without much difficulty, either from the many inscriptions mentioning the place or from the subjects shown in the windows, which included several clearly defined series of scenes or stories.

The passage that opened my story had put the antiquary on the trail of another identification. In a private chapel—never mind where—he had seen three large figures. Each filled a whole panel of a window, and all were clearly the work of one artist. Their style showed that the artist was a sixteenth-century German, but until now their precise place of origin had been a puzzle. They represented—will it surprise you?—JOB THE PATRIARCH, JOHN THE EVANGELIST and ZECHARIAH THE PROPHET. Each held a book or scroll bearing a sentence from his writings. Naturally, the antiquary had copied these and noticed how oddly they differed from every version of the Latin Vulgate Bible he had examined. Job’s scroll read, ‘There is a place for gold where it is hidden’, with ‘hidden’ replacing ‘smelted’. John’s book read, ‘They have on their garments a writing that no one knows’, altering ‘written on his garment’ and taking the following words from another verse. Zechariah’s read, ‘Upon one stone are seven eyes.’ This alone of the three was an unaltered biblical text.

Our investigator had been greatly puzzled by the grouping of these three figures in one window. They had no historical, symbolic or doctrinal connection. He could only suppose that they had belonged to a very large series of Prophets and Apostles, perhaps filling all the high windows of some spacious church. But the passage in the Sertum changed matters. It showed that Abbot Thomas von Eschenhausen of Steinfeld had constantly spoken the names of the very figures now in Lord D——’s chapel. It also showed that he had installed a painted window in the south aisle of his abbey church, probably around 1520. It was hardly a wild guess that these three figures might have formed part of his gift. Another careful examination of the glass could probably confirm or disprove it. Mr Somerton had plenty of free time, so he lost little time in making his pilgrimage to the private chapel. His guess was fully confirmed. Not only did the style and technique fit the required date and place perfectly, but another window in the chapel contained glass known to have been bought with the three figures. In it he found Abbot Thomas von Eschenhausen’s coat of arms.

During his research, Mr Somerton was repeatedly haunted by memories of the gossip about the hidden treasure. The more he thought about it, the clearer it seemed that, if the Abbot’s puzzling answer meant anything, it meant the secret was somewhere in the window he had installed in the abbey church. Besides, the first of those strangely chosen texts on the scrolls could undeniably be read as a reference to hidden treasure.

He therefore recorded with the greatest care every feature or mark that might help solve the riddle he felt sure the Abbot had left for future generations. Back at his Berkshire manor house, he burnt many a pint of midnight oil over his sketches and tracings. After two or three weeks, the day came when Mr Somerton told his servant to pack both their things for a short journey abroad. For the moment, we will not follow him there.
II

One fine autumn morning, Mr Gregory, the Rector of Parsbury, strolled out before breakfast to the gate of his carriage drive. He meant to meet the postman and breathe the cool air, and achieved both aims. His young children had come with him and were cheerfully asking all sorts of questions. He had barely answered ten or eleven before the postman appeared. Among that morning’s letters was one with a foreign postmark and stamp, which immediately became the subject of eager competition among the young Gregorys. The address was written in an uneducated but plainly English hand.
The Rector opened it and looked at the signature. He recognised the writer as the trusted valet of his friend and local squire, Mr Somerton. The letter read:

RESPECTED SIR, I am very anxious about my master and am writing at his request to beg you to be so kind as to come over. My master has had a nasty shock and is keeping to his bed. I’ve never known him like this, but it’s no wonder, and nothing will do but you, sir. My master asks me to mention that the shortest way here is to drive to Cobblince and take a small carriage. I hope I have made everything clear, but I am very confused myself with anxiety and being awake at night. If I may be so bold, sir, it will be a pleasure to see an honest British face among all these foreign ones.

I remain, sir,
Your obedient servant,
William Brown.
P.S.—The village—I wouldn’t call it a town—is named Steenfeld.

I must leave the reader to imagine in detail the surprise, confusion and hurried preparations such a letter would cause in a quiet Berkshire rectory in the year of Our Lord 1859. It is enough to say that Mr Gregory caught a train to town that day, secured a cabin on the Antwerp boat and a seat on the Coblentz train. From there, it was not difficult to arrange the journey to Steinfeld.

I face a serious disadvantage in telling this story: I have never been to Steinfeld. Neither of the two main participants, who gave me my information, could provide more than a vague and rather gloomy idea of the place. I gather it is small, with a large church stripped of its old fittings. Several large, rather ruined buildings surround the church, most dating from the seventeenth century. At that time its inhabitants rebuilt the abbey in luxurious style, as happened at most abbeys on the Continent. I have not thought it worth spending money on a visit. The place is probably much more attractive than either Mr Somerton or Mr Gregory thought, but there is evidently little, if anything, of outstanding interest to see. Except, perhaps, one thing, which I would not care to see.

The inn where the English gentleman and his servant were staying is—or was—the only acceptable one in the village. Mr Gregory’s driver took him straight there, and he found Mr Brown waiting at the door. At home in Berkshire, Brown was a model of that impassive, whiskered breed known as confidential valets. Here, in a light tweed suit, he was entirely out of his element: anxious, almost irritable, and plainly anything but in control. His relief at seeing his Rector’s ‘honest British face’ was immeasurable, but he could not find words to express it. All he could say was:
“Well, I am pleased to see you, sir, I’m sure. And I’m sure my master will be too.”
“How is your master, Brown?” Mr Gregory asked eagerly.
“I think he’s better, sir, thank you. But he’s had a dreadful time. I hope he’s getting some sleep now, but—”
“What’s been the matter? I couldn’t make it out from your letter. Was there some kind of accident?”

“Well, sir, I hardly know whether I ought to speak about it. My master was very particular that he should be the one to tell you. But no bones are broken. That’s one thing I’m sure we ought to be thankful—”
“What does the doctor say?” Mr Gregory asked.

By then they were outside Mr Somerton’s bedroom, speaking quietly. Mr Gregory happened to be in front. Feeling for the handle, he accidentally ran his fingers over the door panels. Before Brown could reply, a terrible cry came from inside.
“In God’s name, who’s that?” were the first words they heard. “Is that you, Brown?”
“Yes, sir. It’s me, sir, and Mr Gregory,” Brown answered quickly. An audible groan of relief came in reply.

They entered the room, which had been darkened against the afternoon sun. Mr Gregory felt a shock of pity at his friend’s usually calm face, now drawn and wet with the sweat of fear. Sitting up in the curtained bed, Somerton held out a shaking hand to welcome him.
“Better for seeing you, my dear Gregory,” he answered the Rector’s first question. It was plainly true.

After five minutes of conversation, Brown later reported, Mr Somerton was more himself than he had been for days. He managed a more than respectable dinner and spoke confidently of being able to face a journey to Coblentz within twenty-four hours.

“But there’s one thing,” he said, with a return of agitation that Mr Gregory was sorry to see, “that I must beg you to do for me, my dear Gregory. Don’t”—he laid his hand on Gregory’s to prevent any interruption—“don’t ask what it is or why I want it done. I’m not well enough to explain yet. It would set me back, undo all the good your coming has done. All I’ll say is that you’ll run no risk whatever, and that Brown can and will show you what to do tomorrow. It’s merely to put back—to keep—something—No, I can’t speak of it yet. Would you mind calling Brown?”

“Well, Somerton,” said Mr Gregory as he crossed to the door, “I won’t ask for explanations until you’re ready to give them. If this business is as easy as you say, I’ll very gladly do it for you first thing in the morning.”
“Ah, I knew you would, my dear Gregory. I was certain I could rely on you. I’ll owe you more thanks than I can express. Now, here’s Brown. A word with you, Brown.”
“Shall I leave?” Mr Gregory put in.

“Not at all. Goodness, no. Brown, first thing tomorrow morning—you don’t mind an early start, I know, Gregory—you must take the Rector to—there, you know.” Brown nodded, looking grave and anxious. “And the two of you will put that back. There’s no need to be alarmed. It’s perfectly safe in daylight. You know what I mean. It’s on the step, you know, where—where we put it.” Brown swallowed dryly once or twice, and, unable to speak, bowed. “And—yes, that’s all. Just one more word, my dear Gregory. If you can refrain from asking Brown about this, I’ll be even more grateful. By tomorrow evening at the latest, if all goes well, I believe I’ll be able to tell you the whole story from beginning to end. Now I’ll wish you goodnight. Brown will stay with me—he sleeps here—and, if I were you, I’d lock my door. Yes, make quite sure of that. They—they prefer it, the people here, and it’s better. Goodnight, goodnight.”

With that, they parted. If Mr Gregory woke once or twice in the early hours and imagined he heard something fumbling around the lower part of his locked door, perhaps that was only to be expected. He was, after all, a quiet man suddenly placed in an unfamiliar bed in the middle of a mystery. Certainly, for the rest of his life he believed he had heard that sound two or three times between midnight and dawn.

He rose with the sun and went out with Brown soon afterwards. Puzzling though Mr Somerton’s request was, the task proved neither difficult nor alarming. Within half an hour of leaving the inn, it was done. I shall not yet reveal what it was.

Later that morning, Mr Somerton, now almost himself again, was able to leave Steinfeld. That evening he settled down to give the promised explanation. Whether this happened at Coblentz or somewhere along the way, I am not certain. Brown was present, but he would never say how much of the matter he really understood, and I cannot guess.
III
This was Mr Somerton’s story:

“You both know, roughly, that I made this journey to investigate something connected with some old painted glass in Lord D——’s private chapel. Well, the whole matter began with this passage in an old printed book. I’d like you to listen to it.”
At this point, Mr Somerton carefully went over ground already familiar to us.

“On my second visit to the chapel,” he continued, “I meant to record everything I could: figures, lettering, scratches made with a diamond point, even marks that seemed accidental. I began with the inscriptions on the scrolls. The first, Job’s—‘There is a place for the gold where it is hidden’—had been deliberately altered. I had no doubt it referred to the treasure, so I turned with some confidence to St John’s: ‘They have on their garments a writing that no one knows.’ You’ll have thought of the obvious question: was there writing on the figures’ robes? I could see none. Each cloak had a broad black border, conspicuous and rather ugly in the window. I admit I was baffled. Without a curious stroke of luck, I think I would have abandoned the search where the canons of Steinfeld had before me. But the glass was very dusty. Lord D—— happened to come in, noticed my blackened hands, and kindly insisted on sending for a round-headed broom to clean the window. I suppose there must have been something rough in the broom. At any rate, as it passed over one cloak’s border, it left a long scratch, and a yellow stain immediately appeared beneath it. I asked the man to stop for a moment and hurried up the ladder to examine the spot. There was the yellow stain, certainly. What had come away was a thick black paint, evidently brushed on after the glass had been fired. It could therefore be scraped off easily without causing damage. So I scraped, and you’ll scarcely believe—no, I do you an injustice; you’ll already have guessed—that beneath the black paint I found two or three clearly formed capital letters, stained yellow on a clear background. Of course, I could hardly contain my delight.

“I told Lord D—— I’d found an inscription that might be very interesting, and asked permission to uncover all of it. He raised no objection whatever and told me to do exactly as I pleased. Then he had to leave for an appointment—rather to my relief, I must admit. I began at once and found it fairly easy. Time had broken down the paint, of course, and it came away almost at a touch. I don’t think it took even two hours altogether to clean the black borders on all three window panels. Just as the inscription said, each figure had ‘writing on its garments that nobody knew’.

“That discovery made me absolutely certain I was on the right track. But what did the inscription say? While cleaning the glass, I had almost deliberately avoided reading the letters, saving the pleasure until I had uncovered them all. When I did, my dear Gregory, I assure you I could almost have cried with disappointment. It was the most hopeless jumble of letters ever shaken up in a hat. Here it is:

Job. DREVICIOPEDMOOMSMVIVLISLCAVIBASBATAOVT
St John. RDIIEAMRLESIPVSPODSEEIRSETTAAESGIAVNNR
Zechariah. FTEEAILNQDPVAIVMTLEEATTOHIOONVMCAAT.H.Q.E.

“For a few minutes I felt utterly blank, and must have looked it, but my disappointment didn’t last. I realised almost at once that I was dealing with a cipher: a coded message. Given its early date, I thought it was likely to be fairly simple. So I copied the letters with the most anxious care. As I did, another small discovery confirmed that belief. After copying the letters on Job’s robe, I counted them to check that I’d got them right. There were thirty-eight. Just as I finished, I noticed a mark scratched with a sharp point on the edge of the border: simply the number xxxviii, thirty-eight in Roman numerals. To cut the story short, each of the other panels had a similar note, if I may call it that. Clearly, Abbot Thomas had given the glass painter very strict instructions about the writing, and the man had taken great care to get it right.

“You can imagine how closely I then examined every part of the glass for further clues. Naturally, I didn’t overlook Zechariah’s scroll: ‘Upon one stone are seven eyes.’ But I soon decided this must refer to a mark on a stone that could only be found at the place where the treasure was hidden. In short, I made every possible note, sketch and tracing, then returned to Parsbury to solve the cipher at my leisure. Oh, the agonies I went through! At first I thought myself very clever. I was certain the key would be found in one of the old books about secret writing. Joachim Trithemius’s Steganographia seemed particularly promising. He had been an earlier contemporary of Abbot Thomas. I obtained that, Selenius’s Cryptographia, Bacon’s de Augmentis Scientiarum, and several others. But I found nothing. Then I tried the ‘most frequent letter’ method, first using Latin as the basis, then German. That didn’t help either; I’m not sure whether it should have. So I returned to the window itself and read through my notes, hoping almost against hope that the Abbot had supplied the key somewhere himself. I could make nothing of the colours or patterns of the robes. There were no landscapes in the background with smaller objects in them, and nothing useful in the canopies. The figures’ poses seemed my only remaining hope. ‘Job,’ I read, ‘scroll in left hand; forefinger of right hand pointing upwards. John: inscribed book in left hand; right hand giving a blessing with two fingers. Zechariah: scroll in left hand; right hand raised like Job’s, but with three fingers pointing up.’ In other words, Job held up one finger, John two, Zechariah three. Could that conceal a numerical key? My dear Gregory”—Mr Somerton laid his hand on his friend’s knee—“that was the key. I couldn’t make it fit at first, but after two or three attempts I saw what was intended. After the inscription’s first letter, skip one letter. After the next, skip two; after that, skip three. Now look at my result. I’ve marked the letters that form words:

[D]R[E]VI[C]IOP[E]D[M]OO[M]SMV[I]V[L]IS[L]CAV[I]B[A]SB[A]TAO[V]T
[R]DI[I]EAM[R]L[E]SI[P]VSP[O]D[S]EE[I]RSE[T]T[A]AE[S]GIA[V]N[N]R
F[T]EEA[I]L[N]QD[P]VAI[V]M[T]LE[E]ATT[O]H[I]OO[N]VMC[A]A[T].H.Q.E.

“Do you see it? ‘Decem millia auri reposita sunt in puteo in at. . .’—‘Ten thousand pieces of gold are stored in a well in…’, followed by an unfinished word beginning at. So far, so good. I tried the same method on the remaining letters, but it didn’t work. I wondered whether the dots after the last three letters might signal a change of method. Then I thought, ‘Wasn’t there something about a well in the account of Abbot Thomas in the Sertum?’ There was: he had built a puteus in atrio—a well in the courtyard. Of course, there was my word, atrio. Next I copied all the remaining letters, leaving out those I had already used. That gave me what you see on this slip:

RVIIOPDOOSMVVISCAVBSBTAOTDIEAMLSIVSPDEERSETAEGIANRFEEALQDVAIMLEATTHOOVM
CA.H.Q.E.

“Now I knew the first three letters I needed: rio, to complete atrio, ‘courtyard’. As you can see, all three occur among the first five letters. The two i’s confused me a little at first, but I soon saw that I must take every other letter from the rest of the inscription. You can work it out yourself. Continuing where the first ‘round’ stopped, it gives this:

‘rio domus abbatialis de Steinfeld a me, Thoma, qui posui custodem super ea. Gare à qui la touche’—‘…courtyard of the abbot’s house at Steinfeld, by me, Thomas, who have set a guardian over them. Let whoever touches it beware.’
“So the whole secret was revealed:
‘Ten thousand pieces of gold are stored in the well in the courtyard of the abbot’s house at Steinfeld by me, Thomas, who have set a guardian over them. Let whoever touches it beware.’

“I should explain that the last words were a motto Abbot Thomas had adopted. I found it with his coat of arms in another piece of glass at Lord D——’s. He had put the whole thing into his cipher, although it doesn’t quite fit grammatically.

“Well, my dear Gregory, what would anyone in my position have been tempted to do? Could anyone have resisted setting off for Steinfeld, as I did, and tracing the secret literally to its fountainhead? I don’t believe so. At any rate, I couldn’t. As you know, I reached Steinfeld as quickly as the resources of civilisation could get me there, and settled into the inn you saw. I must admit I had some misgivings: on one side, disappointment; on the other, danger. The Abbot’s well might have been completely destroyed. Or someone who knew nothing about ciphers might, through sheer luck, have found the treasure before me. And then”—his voice shook quite noticeably—“I’ll admit I was uneasy about what those words concerning the treasure’s guardian meant. But, if you don’t mind, I’ll say no more about that until—until I must.

“Brown and I began exploring as soon as we could. Naturally, I had said I was interested in the abbey’s remains, so we had to visit the church, impatient though I was to be elsewhere. Still, I was interested in seeing the windows where the glass had been, especially the one at the eastern end of the south aisle. To my surprise, some fragments and coats of arms survived in the small panels within its decorative stonework. There was Abbot Thomas’s shield, and a small figure holding a scroll that read, ‘They have eyes, and will not see’ (‘They have eyes, and will not see’). I take that to have been the Abbot’s little dig at his canons.

“But of course, the main object was to find the Abbot’s house. As far as I know, a monastery’s plan gives it no fixed position. You can’t predict that it will be east of the cloister, as you can with the chapter house, or that it will connect with one of the church’s cross-arms, as the dormitory does. I thought too many questions might stir up lingering memories of the treasure, so I decided to try finding it myself first. The search was neither long nor difficult. It was that three-sided courtyard south-east of the church that you saw this morning, with abandoned masses of buildings round it and grass growing through the paving. I was very glad it was unused, not far from our inn, and overlooked by no inhabited building. There were only orchards and paddocks on the slopes east of the church. I can tell you, that fine stone glowed wonderfully in Tuesday afternoon’s rather watery yellow sunset.

“Next came the well. There was little doubt about that, as you can confirm. It really is remarkable. I think the stone rim is Italian marble, and I thought the carving must be Italian too. You may remember the relief carvings of Eliezer and Rebekah, Jacob opening the well for Rachel, and similar subjects. But the Abbot had carefully avoided any of his mocking inscriptions full of hints—presumably to prevent suspicion.

“Of course, I examined the entire structure with the greatest interest. The well-head was square, with an opening in one side and an arch over it. On the arch was a wheel for the rope, evidently still in very good condition. It had been used within the last sixty years, perhaps much more recently, though not very recently. Then there were the questions of depth and how to get inside. I suppose it was between sixty and seventy feet deep. As for access, it almost seemed the Abbot wanted to lead searchers to the very door of his treasure chamber. As you tested for yourself, large stone blocks were built securely into the masonry, forming a regular staircase that spiralled round and round the inside of the well.

“It almost seemed too good to be true. I wondered whether it was a trap: perhaps the stones were arranged to tip over when weight was put on them. But I tested quite a few with my own weight and my stick. They all seemed perfectly firm, and were. Naturally, I decided that Brown and I would try our experiment that very night.

“I was well prepared. Knowing what sort of place I would have to explore, I had brought plenty of good rope, webbing straps to go round my body, and crossbars to hold on to. I also had lanterns, candles and crowbars. Everything would fit into a single carpetbag without arousing suspicion. I checked that my rope was long enough and that the bucket wheel worked properly. Then we went back for dinner.

“I had a cautious little conversation with the landlord. From it, I gathered he wouldn’t be too surprised if I went out with my servant at about nine for a stroll, to make—Heaven forgive me!—a sketch of the abbey by moonlight. I asked nothing about the well, and I’m unlikely to now. I imagine I know as much about it as anyone in Steinfeld. At least”—he shuddered violently—“I don’t want to know any more.

“Now we come to the crisis. I hate thinking about it, but I’m sure, Gregory, that recalling it exactly as it happened will be better for me in every way. Brown and I set off with our bag at about nine. We attracted no attention, managing to slip out of the back of the inn yard into an alley that took us right to the edge of the village. Within five minutes we reached the well. We sat on its rim for a little while to make sure no one was about or watching us. All we heard were some horses grazing out of sight further down the eastern slope. No one saw us, and the splendid full moon gave us plenty of light to fit the rope properly over the wheel. Then I secured the strap round my body beneath my arms. We fastened the rope’s end very firmly to a ring in the stonework. Brown took the lit lantern and followed me; I carried a crowbar. We began cautiously descending, feeling each step before standing on it and searching the walls for a marked stone.

“I counted the steps half aloud as we descended. We reached the thirty-eighth before I noticed anything at all uneven in the masonry. Even there, I saw no mark. I began to feel lost, wondering whether the Abbot’s cipher might be an elaborate hoax. At the forty-ninth step, the staircase ended. With a sinking heart, I started back up. When I reached the thirty-eighth again, with Brown and his lantern a step or two above me, I examined that little irregularity as closely as I could. There was not the slightest sign of a mark.

“Then I noticed that the surface looked just a little smoother than the rest—or at least different in some way. Perhaps it was cement rather than stone. I struck it hard with my iron bar. It sounded distinctly hollow, though perhaps that was simply because we were in a well. But there was more. A large flake of cement fell onto my feet, exposing marks on the stone beneath. I had tracked the Abbot down, my dear Gregory. Even now, I feel a certain pride in it. A few more taps removed all the cement, revealing a stone slab about two feet square with a cross carved on it. Another disappointment, but only for a moment. You reassured me with a casual remark, Brown. If I remember correctly, you said:
“‘That’s a strange cross. It looks like a lot of eyes.’

“I snatched the lantern from your hand and saw, with more pleasure than I can express, that the cross consisted of seven eyes: four in a vertical line and three horizontally. The last scroll in the window was explained just as I had expected. Here was my ‘stone with the seven eyes’. So far, the Abbot’s information had been exact. As I thought of that, my anxiety about the ‘guardian’ returned more strongly than ever. Still, I wasn’t going to turn back now.

“Without giving myself time to think, I knocked away the cement around the marked stone, then prised at its right side with my crowbar. It moved at once. I saw it was only a thin, light slab, easily lifted out by one person, blocking the entrance to a hollow space. I lifted it out without breaking it and put it on the step. Being able to replace it might be very important to us. Then I waited several minutes on the step above. I don’t know why, but I think I was waiting to see whether something dreadful would rush out. Nothing happened. Next I lit a candle and placed it very cautiously inside the opening. I meant partly to test for bad air, partly to glimpse what was inside. There was some bad air: it nearly put the flame out. But before long the candle burnt steadily. The hollow extended a little way back and to both the right and left of its entrance. Inside were some rounded, pale objects that might be bags. There was no point waiting. I faced the opening and looked in. Nothing lay directly in front of it. I reached my arm inside and felt very cautiously to the right…
“Just give me a glass of cognac, Brown. I’ll continue in a moment, Gregory…

“Well, I felt to the right. My fingers touched something curved that felt—yes—more or less like leather. It was rather damp, and clearly part of something heavy and full. I must say, there seemed nothing to alarm anyone. I grew bolder, reached in with both hands as well as I could, and pulled it towards me. It moved. Though heavy, it came more easily than I had expected. As I pulled it towards the opening, my left elbow knocked over the candle and put it out. I brought the thing directly in front of the entrance and began pulling it through. Just then Brown gave a sharp exclamation and ran quickly up the steps with the lantern. He’ll tell you why in a moment. Startled, I looked round after him. I saw him stand for a minute at the top, then walk a few yards away. Then I heard him call softly, ‘All right, sir,’ and went on pulling out the great bag in complete darkness. It caught for an instant on the edge of the hole, then slid forwards onto my chest and put its arms round my neck.

“My dear Gregory, I’m telling you the exact truth. I believe I now know the utmost terror and revulsion a man can endure without losing his mind. Even now, I can barely tell you the outline of what happened. I was aware of a horrible smell of mould, and a cold sort of face pressed against my own, moving slowly over it. Several—I don’t know how many—legs, arms, tentacles, or something clung to my body. Brown says I screamed like a beast. I fell backwards off my step, and the creature slipped down, I suppose, onto that same step. Providentially, the strap round me held firm. Brown kept his head and was strong enough to pull me up to the top and over the rim quite quickly. Exactly how he did it, I don’t know, and I think he’d find it hard to tell you. I believe he managed to hide our equipment in the abandoned building nearby. With great difficulty, he got me back to the inn. I was in no condition to explain, and Brown knows no German. Next morning, however, I told them some story about a bad fall in the abbey ruins, which I suppose they believed. Before I continue, I’d like you to hear what happened to Brown during those few minutes. Tell the Rector what you told me, Brown.”

“Well, sir,” Brown said, speaking quietly and nervously, “this is just how it happened. My master was busy in front of the hole. I was holding the lantern and watching when I heard something drop into the water—from the top, I thought. So I looked up and saw someone’s head looking over at us. I suppose I must have said something. I held up the light and ran up the steps, and it shone straight onto his face. That was a bad one, sir, if ever I saw one! An elderly man, with a very sunken face, and laughing, I thought. I got up those steps almost as quickly as I’m telling you, but when I reached the ground there wasn’t a sign of anyone. Nobody could have got away in that time, let alone an old man. I made sure he wasn’t crouching beside the well or anything. Next I heard my master give a horrible cry. All I could see was him hanging from the rope. As he says, I couldn’t tell you how I got him up.”
“You hear that, Gregory?” Mr Somerton asked. “Now, can you think of any explanation?”

“The whole thing is so ghastly and strange that I admit I can scarcely think straight. But it did occur to me that perhaps the—well, the person who set the trap had come to see how well his plan had worked.”

“Exactly, Gregory, exactly. I can think of nothing else so—likely, I would say, if that word belonged anywhere in this story. I think it must have been the Abbot… Well, there isn’t much more to tell. I had a miserable night, with Brown sitting up beside me. Next day I was no better and couldn’t get up. There was no doctor available, and I doubt one could have done much for me anyway. I made Brown write to you, then endured a second terrible night. And of this I’m certain, Gregory. I think it affected me more than the first shock, because it lasted longer: someone or something watched outside my door all night. I almost think there were two. It wasn’t just the faint noises I heard from time to time throughout the hours of darkness. There was the smell—the hideous smell of mould. I had taken off every rag I wore that first evening and made Brown remove them. I believe he stuffed them into his room’s stove. Yet the smell remained, as strong as it had been in the well, and what’s more, it came from outside the door. With the first glimmer of dawn, it faded, and the sounds stopped too. That convinced me the thing—or things—were creatures of darkness that couldn’t bear daylight. So I felt sure that, if someone could replace the stone, it—or they—would be powerless until someone removed it again. I had to wait for you to do that. Naturally, I couldn’t send Brown alone, and still less could I tell anyone from the village.
“Well, that’s my story. If you don’t believe it, I can’t help that. But I think you do.”

“Indeed,” said Mr Gregory, “I see no alternative. I must believe it! I saw the well and the stone myself. I thought I glimpsed the bags—or something else—in the hole. And to be frank, Somerton, I believe something watched outside my door last night too.”
“It may well have, Gregory. But thank goodness that’s over. By the way, is there anything you can tell me about your visit to that dreadful place?”

“Very little,” he answered. “Brown and I put the slab back easily enough. He secured it firmly with the iron pieces and wedges you’d asked him to get. We managed to smear the surface with mud so it looks just like the rest of the wall. I did notice one thing among the carvings on the well-head that I think you must have missed. A horrible, grotesque shape—perhaps more like a toad than anything else. Beside it was a label with two Latin words: ‘Depositum custodi’—‘Guard what has been entrusted to you.’”
